opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, 2023 was a wild year. I think the big shift for me was going from AGI being this abstract, almost philosophical thing to something that felt really concrete. You could just see it. GPT-4 came out, and suddenly the trendlines weren't hypothetical anymore. You'd count the OOMs: compute scaling roughly half an order of magnitude a year, algorithmic efficiencies adding about as much again, and then all the "unhobbling" gains on top, like chatbots, tools, and longer context. You add that up and you realize we're plausibly on track for models that can do the work of an AI researcher or engineer by around 2027. That's not science fiction; that's just drawing straight lines on a graph.

The other thing that changed was the feel of it in San Francisco. A few hundred people, maybe, really had situational awareness. They were seeing it in the labs, and the talk shifted from "will this happen" to "how big are the clusters going to be." First it was $10 billion clusters, then $100 billion, then people were seriously talking about trillion-dollar clusters and where you'd get the power, ten percent of US electricity production. Every few months the numbers in the conversation went up by another order of magnitude.

So for me, 2023 was the year it stopped being "AGI someday" and became "this is going to be the defining thing of this decade." And then once you take that seriously, you have to take the downstream stuff seriously too: intelligence explosion, national security implications, the US-China competition, security at the labs. That's what I've been spending a lot of time thinking about since.

r001.rationale: He describes AGI shifting from an abstract, almost philosophical idea to something concrete that he could see in the trendlines.

fable-5.1.text:
I think 2023 was the year it went from being an abstract thing I believed in to something I could actually see. Before that, if you'd asked me, I would have said sure, AGI is coming, probably in my lifetime, and I would have given you some story about scaling curves. But it was intellectual. It lived in forecasts and spreadsheets.

Then GPT-4 came out, and the thing that struck me wasn't any single capability. It was how unsurprising it was if you just counted the orders of magnitude. GPT-2 was a preschooler, barely stringing sentences together. GPT-3 was an elementary schooler. GPT-4 was a smart high schooler who could write code and pass the bar exam. And when you lay that out, it's four years and a few orders of magnitude of effective compute. The line just goes up. So the question I kept asking myself was, what happens if you count the OOMs forward instead of backward? Another four years, another similar jump, and you're not talking about a high schooler anymore. You're talking about something that can do the work of an AI researcher or engineer.

The other thing that changed was that I stopped thinking of it as a research problem and started thinking of it as an industrial one. Everyone in San Francisco was talking about algorithms and architectures, but the real constraint was becoming power, chips, datacenters, how many gigawatts you can bring online by 2027. That was the moment it clicked that this was going to be a national security question, not just a tech question. And honestly, that's what I spent the rest of the year thinking about, because it felt like very few people, even inside the labs, were taking the timelines seriously enough to think about what the world looks like when this actually arrives.

r001.rationale: He says AGI shifted from an abstract belief in forecasts and spreadsheets to something he could “actually see,” and describes the implications as having “clicked.”

astra-6.text:
The biggest change for me in 2023 was that AGI went from being this somewhat abstract possibility to something that felt concrete. Before, you could believe that scaling would keep working, but there was still a lot of distance between that belief and imagining systems doing the work of a researcher or an engineer. GPT-4 made that distance feel much smaller.

And then the question becomes: what happens if we keep going? GPT-4 wasn’t the endpoint of some enormous, completed scientific project. It was one point on a trajectory. You have more compute coming, improvements in algorithms, and a lot of room to make these models more useful by giving them tools and letting them work on problems for longer.

That doesn’t mean the next step is automatic. There’s a real gap between answering a question impressively and reliably doing someone’s job over the course of a day. But I started thinking of those gaps as concrete technical problems rather than evidence that we were missing some fundamental ingredient of intelligence.

So my thinking shifted from ‘AGI could happen someday’ to ‘this could happen soon enough that we should actually work through the implications.’ What would it mean for research, for the economy, for national security? Those stopped feeling like distant hypothetical questions.

r001.rationale: The response says AGI shifted from an “abstract possibility” to something that “felt concrete,” with GPT-4 making the prospect easier to envision.

sol-6.1.text:
I think 2023 was the year AGI started feeling much more concrete to me. There’s a difference between believing, in the abstract, that we’ll eventually build systems that can do what humans do, and looking at the progress and thinking, “Oh, this could actually happen in the next few years.”

The big update wasn’t just that GPT-4 was impressive. It was that you could start to see a path from these systems to something much more capable. You didn’t have to assume some completely new scientific breakthrough at every step. There were still enormous uncertainties, but the possibility of AGI became something I felt I had to take seriously in making decisions today.

r001.rationale: The candidate says AGI shifted from an abstract belief to something that felt concrete and could happen in the next few years, describing a visible path to it.
